summary:
Mission Patch is a browser game by team Ad Astra Per Aspera. Players design, build, launch and fly their own NASA-style science missions.

Players choose one of ten missions, from a student CubeSat to a Titan drone. They pick an orbit, each with real numbers worked out using NASA’s GMAT tool. Then they pick a rocket whose payload capacity changes with the destination. Next they drag parts onto a 3D spacecraft, balancing mass, power, budget, data, communications and time, with each mission’s critical resources highlighted. A design review based on JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels flags anything that won’t work. Then comes a launch with real telemetry and a chance of failure, a flight past debris and radiation, and a science stage: aiming instruments, landing, building a station or steering robots under real signal delays.

This tackles the challenge head-on: every trade-off it describes, such as orbit choice, launch vehicle limits and resource balancing, decides whether a mission succeeds. It matters because real mission design is usually hidden from the public. details:
Mission Patch is a browser game that takes players through the whole life of a NASA-style science mission:

  1. Choose a mission. There are ten, from a student CubeSat photographing Earth to a drone flying on Saturn’s moon Titan. Each has a budget, a deadline, required instruments and highlighted critical resources.
  2. Plan. Pick an orbit (low Earth, geostationary, Lagrange points, the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, the Sun’s corona, Titan) and a rocket. Every orbit explains its trade-offs in coverage, sunlight, communications and lifetime. Rockets differ in cost, reliability and how much they can lift to each destination.
  3. Build. Drag parts onto a 3D spacecraft: structure, power, batteries, communications, computers, attitude control and instruments. A live panel tracks mass, power, budget, data, communications and time.
  4. Review. A green/yellow/red checklist based on JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels must be cleared before launch.
  5. Launch and fly. Live telemetry follows a real launch profile, and launches can fail. In orbit, players dodge debris, radiation waves and solar flares.
  6. Do the science. Aim instruments at targets, land on other worlds, build a station, drive a rover through signal delay, melt through Europa’s ice, or strike an asteroid moonlet as NASA’s DART mission did.

Benefits

  • It runs in any web browser, on computers, tablets and phones, with no install.
  • It is playable by all ages, with a guided tutorial and four difficulty modes.
  • Failure teaches: the review and failed launches explain why something went wrong and how to fix it.
  • Real science is built in. Orbit figures come from NASA’s GMAT tool, planets and stars from GMAT’s data, and players can view real NASA spacecraft in 3D.
  • Replay value comes from a Tech Shop of unlockable parts, bonus challenges and mission patches to collect.

Intended impact

We want players to understand that every mission is a series of trade-offs, and to inspire students to explore science, engineering and careers in space. Teachers can use it in classrooms to show how missions are designed.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, delivered as a single self-contained file.
  • Graphics: three.js for the 3D spacecraft builder and the NASA model viewer, and the HTML Canvas for the flight and science games.
  • Sound: the Web Audio API generates every sound effect, including NASA’s real “Quindar” radio tones.
  • Data: NASA GMAT R2026a (planet maps, star catalog and physical constants), NASA 3D Resources models, the NASA Design and Develop a Science Mission guide, and JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels paper.
  • Fonts: Space Grotesk and Inter from Google Fonts.
  • Hardware: none required beyond a device with a browser.
  • AI assistance: we used Claude, an AI assistant by Anthropic, to help write and test code.

Creativity

  • Mission patches, a real NASA tradition, serve as rewards.
  • Each new mission has its own gimmick: a first-person asteroid impact, keeping a heat shield facing the Sun, flying a Titan drone between recharges, and exploring a pitch-dark lunar cave by headlight.
  • A 3D spacecraft is built by snapping parts onto realistic mounting points.
  • The sound design echoes real mission control.
  • Fictional gear is clearly labelled as fiction, next to real-world facts for every real part.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: keyboard controls, reduced-motion support, readable text and plain English for all ages.
  • Accuracy versus fun: real physics ratios and orbit data, with costs and signal delays scaled down so the game stays playable.
  • Balance: we tested every difficulty mode with automated players.
  • Performance and offline use: a single file of about 750 KB that loads quickly.
  • Credit: all NASA and open-source sources are attributed.
